archetype.name: Playoff Team (offense-first)
archetype.definition: A team whose league-best offense and elite special teams carry a defense ranked near the bottom, with a 7-1 record that runs a couple of wins ahead of its underlying margin.

report.headline: The league's best offense is covering for a defense that bends and misses tackles
report.take:
Buffalo under first-year coach Joe Brady looks like the Bills of the last half-decade on one side of the ball and nothing like them on the other. The offense leads the league in EPA per play (0.169) and in scoring, which fits a franchise that has finished top four in offensive EPA in most recent seasons. The defense is the break from history: 29th in EPA allowed, when Buffalo's defense ranked 12th or better in every season from 2018 through 2025. This is a new defensive identity, not a slow start from a familiar one.

The offense has changed shape, too. Buffalo passes less than the situation predicts (pass rate over expected of -4.8, 25th), and the run game justifies it: first in rushing success rate, second in yards before contact, fourth in stuff rate. James Cook's 169 carries, plus Josh Allen's legs, make this a ground-and-pound team that also has Allen throwing for a top-three pass EPA. Special teams are a weapon as well, second in EPA per game, and Brady has gone for it on every fourth down the model flagged. It is aggressive, efficient football that scores in waves.

The record flatters the team. The point differential of 69 implies about 5.3 wins, and the Bills have 7, helped by winning four of five one-score games and +1.7 wins over expected, sixth-most in the league. Five of the first six games were shootouts in which Buffalo allowed 29 or more points. The defense creates pressure at the second-best rate in the league, but it finishes sacks at a bottom-tier rate, and its 11.1% missed-tackle rate (30th) turns short completions into long drives. A play-by-play split that strips out some game context grades the defense closer to average (17th), so the true level is probably bad rather than disastrous. Penalties (8.6 a game, 30th) are the other self-inflicted leak.

The last two games hinted at a turn: 10 and 6 points allowed, three takeaways each time. Those came against Baltimore and a Minnesota offense ranked 31st, though, so treat it as a promising sample rather than proof. With Kansas City, Green Bay, Chicago and Denver all on the back half, the defense will get a real test. The offense makes Buffalo a favorite almost every week. Whether this becomes a January team depends on whether the tackling and the finishing of pressures catch up.

strengths.title: An offense that wins every way
strengths.body: Buffalo leads the league in offensive EPA and yards per game, and does it with balance: a top-three pass EPA alongside a run game that ranks third in rush EPA. The run-first tendency is earned, not stubborn, since the line gives backs the second-most yards before contact. Allen and this offensive standard have held up across several seasons, so this is the most bankable part of the team.

strengths.title: A line that wins up front
strengths.body: The offensive line ranks first in run success rate and fourth in stuff rate, and it allows a sack rate in the top half despite Allen holding the ball a bit longer than most. That line is why the Bills could run for 200-plus yards against Detroit and the Rams. It is also the unit most exposed to injury right now, with Dion Dawkins, a 99% snap starter, listed out.

strengths.title: Hidden yards on special teams
strengths.body: Special teams add 4.29 EPA a game, second in the league. Combined with a coach who has gone for it on every recommended fourth down, Buffalo squeezes extra possessions and points out of the margins. Special-teams value swings year to year, but the fourth-down aggression is a coaching choice and should stick.

concerns.title: Defense allows too much success
concerns.body: Opponents succeed on 47.2% of plays against Buffalo, 29th, and the pass defense ranks 25th in EPA allowed. The deep defense is fine (ninth); the damage comes underneath, where a 30th-ranked missed-tackle rate turns completions into chunk gains and third downs into first downs. This defense ranked 12th or better in every season since 2018, so this is a real flaw in the new scheme, not long-standing noise.

concerns.title: Record ahead of the margin
concerns.body: The point differential implies about 5.3 wins against an actual 7. Buffalo has won four of five one-score games and sits sixth in wins over expected. Close-game luck tends to even out, and a defense that keeps games within a score invites more coin flips down the stretch.

concerns.title: Pressure that doesn't finish
concerns.body: The pass rush pressures at the second-highest rate and hits quarterbacks at the fourth-highest, yet ranks 27th in sacks. That gap usually narrows in the defense's favor over time, which is the main reason to expect some improvement. Paired with 8.6 penalties a game, though, it is a sign of a defense that loses plays it should win.

trend.note: The first six games were shootouts in which the defense allowed 29 or more in five of them. The last two held Baltimore to 10 and Minnesota to 6 with three takeaways each, but Minnesota's offense ranks 31st, so the improvement is real on the scoreboard and unproven against good offenses.

nextGame.headline: Buffalo's passing attack meets a Jets pass defense near the bottom
nextGame.body:
The Book has Buffalo -8.5 at New York with a 50.5 total and a -550 moneyline, and the matchup supports it. The Jets defend the run well (10th in rush EPA allowed) but rank 30th against the pass and 31st against short throws. That invites Buffalo to lean more on Allen's arm than it usually does. On the other side, the Jets' line has allowed 28 sacks, 29th, which sets up Buffalo's pressure-heavy rush to finally finish some plays. The Jets' offense is middling (17th) and has lost four of its five one-score games.

Availability tilts further toward Buffalo. The Jets lose Garrett Wilson, an 89% snap receiver and their top target, along with edge Joseph Ossai and several depth defenders. Buffalo's issue is up front: left tackle Dion Dawkins, a 99% snap starter, is listed out with ribs, and backup tackle Alec Anderson is also out. DT Greg Gaines is out, and CB Jordan Hancock has been designated to return from injured reserve.

waysToWin.title: Attack the Jets' short pass defense
waysToWin.body: New York ranks 31st in EPA allowed on short passes and 30th against the pass overall, while its run defense is solid. Quick throws to Khalil Shakir and Dalton Kincaid let Allen move the ball without asking a patched-up line to hold up on long drops. The Jets also rank 26th in production allowed to tight ends, a direct opening for Kincaid.

waysToWin.title: Pressure turns into sacks
waysToWin.body: Buffalo's pressure rate ranks second, and the Jets give up sacks at the 26th-ranked rate. This is the most likely game for the rush to convert hits into drive-killers. That shortens the field for the league's top offense and protects a defense that struggles once plays extend.

waysToWin.title: Jets without their top receiver
waysToWin.body: With Wilson out, the Jets lose the WR1 role that has been Buffalo's soft spot all year, since opposing WR1s have scored well above their averages against the Bills. Removing that player takes away the matchup most likely to punish Buffalo's coverage.

waysToLose.title: Giveaways hand the Jets short fields
waysToLose.body: Buffalo turned it over five times against the Chargers and twice in each of three other games. The Jets rank 14th in turnover margin and have only lost to the Bills' level of opponent when given help. Extra Jets possessions on short fields are the most realistic path to an upset, given how much the Buffalo defense bends.

waysToLose.title: Running into the Jets' strength
waysToLose.body: Buffalo's run-first habit meets a Jets run defense ranked 10th in EPA allowed, with a top-five tackling rate. Without Dawkins, sticking to the ground could stall drives and turn a comfortable game into a one-score grind, the kind of game New England already won in Buffalo.

waysToLose.title: Penalties and missed tackles extend drives
waysToLose.body: Buffalo ranks 30th in both penalties per game and missed-tackle rate. Those leaks let even a middling offense string together long drives. In a division road game, that can keep the Jets in it into the fourth quarter.

nextGame.watch: How Buffalo's pass protection holds without Dawkins, and whether Brady leans into the short passing game the Jets can't defend instead of the run they can.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense is the part to trust: a top-four offensive EPA is a Buffalo constant, and the run game's success is built on line play rather than game script. Expect scoring to dip a little from the current pace as the schedule stiffens with Kansas City, Green Bay, Chicago, Denver and a trip to New England. Three games against Miami and the Jets offer soft landings. The close-game record should cool, with the point differential suggesting this is closer to a 5-to-6-win team through eight games than a 7-1 juggernaut.

The defense is the swing. Its pressure rate suggests more sacks and turnovers ahead, and the last two games point the right way, but the tackling and success-rate numbers are a real problem that good offenses will test. A winning division title run looks likely given a 7-1 start in a weak AFC East. Seeding against the conference's best depends on that defense settling closer to average.
swingFactors: Whether the pass rush converts pressure into sacks and takeaways
Dawkins' health and the line's pass protection
Tackling against KC, GB, CHI and DEN

confidence.note: Eight games under a new coach; defensive gains came against weak offenses.
